s17.slug: SATURDAY · 7:35 AM · I-10 EAST, SONORA → JUNCTION — MARGOT’S GIDEON
body: East of Sonora the sun is coming up straight down the windshield, low and white-gold, and it lays the Edwards Plateau out ahead of the Odyssey in long blue shadows: live oaks in the draws, cedar on the rises, road cuts of pale limestone stacked like pages. In the median a doe and two yearlings are grazing with their backs to the interstate. Pickups pass the van at eighty, a dog’s head out of every second window, and Kevin holds the right lane at sixty-five with both hands on the wheel and lets Texas go around him.

He put the mix back in at first light, without announcing it, the way he took it out at Phoenix, and the Odyssey has its music again, turned low for the sleepers. Theo is one of them, folded against the left-hand window in the camel coat with his collar up around his ears.

Jack is saying the penance. He has the part he was given and no more: two by two, a walking stick, no bread, no bag, no money in the belt. At the sandals the thread runs out, as it did yesterday at the Rincon, and he goes back to *two by two* and starts over, lips going, his shoulder against the cool of the glass.

In the front seat Margot has turned the visor mirror down and cocked it at the middle row. “Costigan,” she says, finding his eyes in it. “You have been doing something with your mouth since Sonora. It is either Scripture or a stroke, and I have made allowances for both.”
“Homework,” Jack says. “From Osei. Mark, chapter six, every morning till I’m home. I’ve got about half of it by heart and nothing to check the rest against.”

Margot does not turn around. A hand comes back between the headrests holding a small green book, cloth gone to the weave at the corners. Inside the front board, over the Gideons’ printed plate, a purple ink stamp: SANTA LUCIA MOTOR COURT. Somewhere on the Big Sur coast a nightstand has a clean rectangle in its dust.
“I’m not lending you God,” Margot says. “I’m lending you a primary source.”
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “that’s theft.”
“It’s distribution. I’m an end user.”

Jack finds the sixth chapter, the thin paper clinging to his thumb, and it isn’t quite the Mark he was given. *Take nothing for their journey, save a staff only,* it says, *no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse; but be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats.* Osei’s had a bag and a second tunic. This one has *scrip*, which he has to get from the context, and two coats. He is wearing Danny’s Carhartt over a Marisol sweatshirt, which on a strict reading is two coats. He decides to take it as a counsel of perfection, and keeps both versions.
*In what place soever ye enter into an house, there abide till ye depart from that place.* Osei’s word was *stay.* This one is *abide*, which is slower and has a rocking chair in it.

Verse thirteen ends and the page doesn’t, and he goes on reading, the way you go past the end of the part of a letter you were told to read. A prisoner named John, put away for telling a king he can’t have his brother’s wife. A birthday. A girl who dances for the table so well that the king swears to her in front of everyone to give her anything she asks, up to half his kingdom. The girl goes out and asks her mother what to ask. *And the king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath’s sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her.* The head comes in on a charger. The girl gives it to her mother.
Jack shuts the book.

Somebody, in some room, has cracked the Gideon’s spine at this chapter, and when he lets go of the cover it opens again by itself on his knee. His eye does what an eye does with an open page and goes to the nearest verse. *Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.*
In the visor mirror Margot’s eyes, which he hadn’t known were on him, go back to her map. “Field note,” she says. “You read it like somebody reading a letter.”

The sun is full up now. It comes across Kevin’s shoulder and lies on the open page, and the small print goes gold, and Jack leaves the Gideon where it fell, open on his knee, while the Odyssey carries it east.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture. Monday night in the Fishbowl: six versions of Wednesday now. One has reached the Classics department. She wouldn’t read me any of them. Thursday night at the van she took the pie on her lap, for science, and told the van about men in some societies who may not speak to their mothers-in-law; everything goes through a third party. Radcliffe-Brown. Then she turned her recorder off. Friday it was eight versions of Wednesday. Then she drove Picacho to El Paso and wouldn’t stop for anything: there’s nowhere to stop, it’s the Chihuahuan Desert. Saturday at sunup she lent me a Gideon from the Santa Lucia Motor Court. Not God. A primary source.

s18.slug: SATURDAY · 9:55 AM · SAN ANTONIO, A TRUCK STOP ON THE EAST SIDE
body: The truck stop on the east side of San Antonio sells breakfast tacos from a steel window beside the lottery machine, foil-wrapped and hot enough to hurt: potato and egg, chorizo and egg, bean and cheese, a plastic thimble of green salsa with each. Over the register a TV has a reporter in a parka standing in a street full of snow, the Capitol dome behind her. No one in line looks up. It is cool and bright out, and the men at the counter are in work shirts with the sleeves pushed up.

They eat at a picnic table bolted to the concrete beside the ice cage, five of them in the clothes they slept in. Kevin is in a quarter-zip that has become a position. Margot is rumpled for the first time in Jack’s experience and has somehow kept every crease in place. Theo has the camel coat. Laney is awake. She has the seat-belt crease down one cheek like a sash and a taco in each hand, and she addresses the table. “My mouth tastes like Oklahoma. I’m not taking questions, comments or eye contact until the second one.”

Theo’s phone goes off on the steel between the salsa and Margot’s maps, a buzz you can feel in the bench. He reads the name on the screen. Theo, who has never in Jack’s sight left a plate unfinished, leaves a bean-and-cheese in its foil. “Excuse me. My mother. Somebody say a prayer, Costigan, it ought to be you.” It’s a good line, and it lands half a tone high. He is on his feet with the phone at his ear before the second buzz, walking, not to the restroom and not to the van but out across the lot between a Peterbilt and a stock trailer, to the far edge, where the pavement gives out into winter grass and a drainage ditch. He turns his back on the picnic table and stops.

The Odyssey sits across the lot at the diesel island with its hatch to them and its side door open. Somebody has gone over the 2 on the back glass with a thumb and made it a 1 and left the S: WHO DAT · 1 DAYS.
At the van, Lena is trying to refold a map that has never in its life been refolded by anyone.

s18t.slug: SATURDAY · 10:00 AM · SAN ANTONIO, THE EDGE OF THE LOT — THE HILL
body: It is a hundred yards to the end of the lot, down a lane of idling reefers, each holding its own diesel note, with grackles lined along the chain-link above them working through every noise they own. Jack hears Theo before he reaches him because Theo isn’t using his phone voice. The phone voice is low and amused and closing on a yacht. This one is high and quick and has no adjectives in it.
He stops by a stack of pallets twenty feet back, where the grass starts. Theo’s camel coat is open in the sun, and his shoulders are up around his ears.

“The hill came down *when*? Before it was *light*? In the *street*. What do you mean, in the — cars? In the storm drains?” A pause. “Who told you to — a *deputy*. Okay. And the barriers, the concrete ones, where are the —” A longer pause. “They *moved?*”
“Mom. Is the house — okay. Okay. And the — no. *Don’t.* Don’t go in it. Let them — Mom. Leave it.”

His free hand comes up and drags down his face from the forehead and stays over his mouth. “Is Poppy with you. Good. Poppy does not get to go back for her shoes. Tell her I said, and tell her I said it nicely.” He listens a long time. “Where are you.” Another silence, shorter. “Bunny’s. In Pasadena. Good. Bunny’s is on a flat. Stay at Bunny’s, stay *there*. I’ll call you tonight. Yes. Okay.”

He takes the phone from his ear and looks at it and presses the button, and stands with it hanging at his side while a reefer cycles on behind him and goes quiet. A trucker at the next trailer is eating a taco off a pocketknife and not looking at anything. Then Theo turns, and his face is already on: the half smile, the weight on one hip, the eyebrows up for business. It takes him a second to find Jack at the pallets, and it doesn’t slip.

“Costigan. You look like a telegram. There isn’t any news.” He puts the phone away in the coat. “My mother’s pool is now a pond. She’s taking it very well. She’s at the Huntington with a Bloody Mary and the dogs.”

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself. Saturday in San Antonio his mother called from a friend’s house in Pasadena: the hill came down in the night. Her pool’s a pond. He told her to leave it. He says she’s at the Huntington with a Bloody Mary and the dogs.

choices.key: In San Antonio Theo’s mother called: the hill came down in the night. You asked if he needed to go home. He said he needs to be in New Orleans.
response: Theo’s mouth is already open on the next thing; Jack can see the shape of it, something with a swizzle stick in it. It closes.
“No,” he says. “I need to be in New Orleans.”
His eyes go to the ditch and come back. He claps Jack on the arm, hard, and they start back across the lot, Theo a half step ahead, the camel coat flapping.

choices.text: “A pond. Lena’s dad will want to stock it.”
choices.key: In San Antonio Theo’s mother called: the hill came down in the night. You told him Lena’s father would want to stock the pond. He laughed.
response: Theo’s head goes back and a bark of laughter comes out of him that he plainly hadn’t arranged. “Redfish,” he says. “He’d want redfish. He’d put in a crab trap and call it a water feature.” He wipes an eye with the heel of his hand and blames the sun. “Tell Tony I’m taking bids.”
They start back across the lot, Theo laughing again at the Peterbilt for no reason it has given him.

choices.text: “That’s twice you’ve told her not to go in the pool house.”
choices.key: In San Antonio Theo’s mother called: the hill came down in the night. You said that was twice he’d told her not to go in. It’s full of mud, he said.
response: Theo smiles at him. It’s a good smile; it has all its teeth.
“It’s full of mud, Costigan,” he says, still smiling. “I don’t want my mother in mud.”
They start back across the lot.
